question: What were the pros and cons of splitting equity equally between Flint founders?
answer_summary: Equal 25% equity split among four Flint founders had pros (equal weight/responsibility, no share disputes, focus on work) and cons (hard decision-making initially — numerous meetings and votes). Solved by trusting data (A/B tested landing pages for product direction) and learning 'disagree but commit'.
text:
Splitting equity equally among four founders at Flint had clear trade-offs.

The upside: everyone carried the same weight and responsibility. There were no disputes over shares, which let us focus entirely on the work.

The downside: decision-making was hard at first — too many meetings and votes. We tried many methodologies before finding what worked. As engineers, we ultimately decided to trust data. We would find ways to get objective signals and committed to following them.

For example, when we disagreed on product direction — generic tool vs specific use case — each founder had a different vision. So we designed separate UIs and landing pages for each idea, released them publicly, measured reactions over a set time period, and followed the most validated path.

That's also where we learned 'disagree but commit': even if your idea lost, you must not work any less because it wasn't chosen.

question: What were the details of the Seed fundraising round at Flint Technologies?

text: We raised a total of roughly KRW 450 million. Strong Ventures and Fast Ventures invested $212K in our Seed Round at a $2.127M post-money valuation, for a 10% equity stake in preferred stock. We also secured a KRW 200 million bank loan guaranteed by KODIT.

question: What structural barriers did you face when fundraising from Korean VCs for Flint?
answer_summary: Two structural barriers made Korean VCs resistant: US incorporation (해외투자신고 bureaucracy, multiple meetings trying to convince us not to incorporate in US) and equal 25% equity split among four founders. Held firm on both — US incorporation was strategically necessary, equal equity was the fair thing to do.
text:
The hardest moment in fundraising was convincing Korean VCs to invest despite two structural barriers.

First, Flint was incorporated in the US. Korean VCs found the 해외투자신고 (overseas investment reporting) bureaucracy burdensome, and we had several meetings where they actively tried to convince us not to incorporate there.

Second, we split equity equally — 25% among all four founders. Korean VCs typically dislike this structure and prefer a clear lead founder.

We held firm on both. US incorporation was strategically necessary for our target market, and equal equity was the fair thing to do since all founders were fully committed and contributing equally.

question: What do you want to receive from Altos?
answer_summary: DJ seeks apprenticeship in judgment through exposure to Altos' decision-making processes, access to diverse portfolio (Baemin, Toss, Furiosa, Anthropic), and hands-on founder support beyond capital.
text:
First, apprenticeship in judgment. Altos has decades of reps through real cycles. I want to learn how your partners build conviction — how you read founders, separate what's structural from what's noise, and stay calm when markets move. Not from a playbook — by being in the room. The conversations, the memos, the actual trade-offs.

Second, the portfolio. Very few funds touch consumer platforms like Baemin and Toss, deep tech like Furiosa and Anthropic, and Korea-US cross-border — all under one roof. That range is the fastest way to build real pattern recognition, because the cases are so different. I want that exposure.

Third, the unglamorous work. Altos is unusual in how it shows up beyond capital. Hiring calibration, GTM sequencing, hard strategic calls — not just writing checks. I want to grow inside a team where helping founders means doing the actual work, with trust and mutual respect.

And I think the fit goes both ways — I bring a founder-operator lens that makes that support real, not theoretical.

question: You started as an engineer — what made you cross over to the business side?
answer_summary: DJ's transition from engineering to business was deliberate, driven by recognizing that bringing technology to market requires fundamentally different skills than building it. TmaxTibero was the turning point where he learned that technical quality matters less than market fit.
text:
My ultimate goal was always to bring technology to market. I've never been interested in technology in isolation—I've been interested in how technology creates real impact in society and in the market.

That's why I intentionally built range early. I studied mechanical engineering to understand real-world systems—mechanics, production processes, manufacturing constraints. At the same time, I studied industrial design to understand the adoption side—design, UI/UX, and why users actually choose a product.

Then I moved into software at TmaxTibero because I believed software would be an essential layer behind almost any modern startup. And that's where the shift really crystallized. Up until then—university and research—technology was something you study and perfect. At Tmax, I saw how technology actually gets deployed into the market. I was the dedicated engineer for Samsung's database migration, and I realized technical quality mattered far less than whether the solution fit the customer's reality—their timeline, risk tolerance, and internal decision-making. That was the first time I understood that bringing technology to market is a fundamentally different skill from building it.

After Tmax, I knew the missing piece in my toolkit was business. I was choosing between two structured paths—joining a strategy consulting firm like McKinsey/BCG/Bain or going into VC—because I wanted to learn market analysis, positioning, and decision-making at scale. But while I was preparing, former colleagues convinced me to start a company with them, and I agreed because there's really nothing better than learning the business side than doing it yourself.

So the transition wasn't a drift away from engineering. It was a deliberate expansion—from building technology to bringing it to market, and owning the full set of decisions that determine whether a product actually wins.

question: What did you learn at TmaxTibero?
answer_summary: At TmaxTibero, DJ learned the gap between research and industry, enterprise dynamics and risk aversion, the value of bridge-building across stakeholders, and critical lessons on leadership, retention, and technical execution in B2B contexts.
text:
I'd group my learning into three personal takeaways, plus one thing I admired and one lesson on leadership.

The gap between research and industry — technology has to earn its existence. Before Tmax, in school and grad research, technology was about proving something can work — one successful experiment out of a hundred is still considered progress. In industry, that mindset flips. At Tmax, I learned technology is judged by purpose and adoption: Why does this exist? Who will pay for it? What pain does it remove? What risk does it reduce? The best implementation doesn't matter if the value isn't clear and the deployment reality doesn't fit the customer.

Enterprise dynamics — buyers optimize for risk, not elegance. Working with large enterprise customers, I learned the decision drivers are rarely "best architecture." They're stability, migration risk, support commitments, security and compliance, and accountability when something breaks. That gave me a lasting filter for evaluating B2B startups: if you can't answer how you de-risk adoption, handle long sales cycles, and survive real-world constraints, the product won't land — no matter how strong the tech is.

Operating as a bridge across three parties. My day-to-day required coordinating a triangle: customer expectations and timelines, internal delivery priorities, and core DB engineering roadmap and API needs. You can't win that with technical skill alone — you win by translating, making trade-offs explicit, and aligning incentives. That bridge capability became the foundation for everything I did later in startups and partnerships.

What I admired. The CTO's level of dedication genuinely impressed me. The company was his life. He ran weekly meetings with every product division — what they were building, where they were stuck — and gave concrete guidance. It was demanding to prepare for, but it raised everyone's bar and helped the whole org level up.

A lesson on leadership and retention. I also learned how critical it is to retain long-tenured product owners — people are the system. When experienced people start leaving, there's always a reason: misalignment on vision, better external opportunities, or incentives that aren't working. And when senior people who hold product context leave — especially with a big senior-junior gap and poor handover — maintenance becomes fragile fast. That taught me something I carry into how I evaluate startups now: I always look at whether the org can retain the people who hold the knowledge, because without that, execution breaks down no matter how good the strategy is.

Overall: Tmax taught me how technology actually earns its place, how enterprises really buy, how to bridge stakeholders — and it gave me a clear view of how leadership intensity and talent retention can make or break execution.

question: What happened to Flint Technologies? Why did you leave?
answer_summary: Flint shut down after two failed pivots. The core lesson: powerful technology doesn't matter without solving behavioral friction. The failure taught DJ a disciplined problem-first approach that later defined his work at DUG.
text:
Flint shut down, and I take responsibility for my part in that. The clean truth is: we made one of the most common mistakes technical founders make — starting from the technology instead of starting from a painful, specific problem. And what's humbling is: I knew startups are supposed to start with the problem. I believed that intellectually. But when you have a powerful technology in your hands, it's surprisingly easy to fall into "we'll find the best use case" mode — and we did.

Our first product was a GNN-based knowledge graph. Technically it was strong, and we saw real early traction — hundreds of users and meaningful usage without marketing. But the core workflow required users to do too much manual work to create and connect information. In demos it looked powerful; in real life it felt like homework. We underestimated the behavior-change barrier, and we didn't remove that friction fast enough. That was a judgment failure, not a technology failure.

After realizing that, we pivoted — but we overcorrected. We went in the opposite direction: a US mobile gifting product inspired by how gifting behavior changed in Korea. We built an MVP on iMessage so users could send small gifts like coffee or dessert. We even based ourselves in New York because it superficially resembled Seoul — dense, walkable, lots of cafes.

But we underestimated market reality: cultural habits were different, merchant infrastructure wasn't standardized, and pricing was messy due to inconsistent menus and taxes. It required too much education and operational coordination to scale, and we couldn't find a path where the economics and rollout became obviously viable within our runway.

At that point, we discussed bootstrapping — but we didn't have a next idea that all of us had real conviction in and were willing to risk years on. So we made the responsible call to shut down, and we agreed we'd reconnect immediately if one of us found a thesis we truly believed in.

The biggest lesson I carried forward is specific: knowing "start from the problem" isn't enough — you have to force that discipline when the tech is tempting. Validate the behavior loop early, and if adoption friction is core, either solve it decisively or stop — because great technology doesn't matter if the behavior doesn't stick.

That's what changed everything at DUG. Every feature, every decision was grounded in user needs — obvious or hidden. I really dove deep into a discipline: What is the problem right now — is it a vitamin or a painkiller? What are people currently doing to remedy that pain — what are the workarounds? If a solution existed, would people actually use it? And most importantly — would they buy it, and for how much? That framework came directly from Flint's failure, and it became how I approached every product decision at DUG.

question: Why did you leave DUG? It's only been a year and a half.
answer_summary: DJ left DUG after 18 months of delivering strong results to pursue VC, recognizing that pattern-matching across multiple companies compounds better than depth in one vertical. The move reflects clarity about his strengths, not instability.
text:
That's a fair question. The honest answer is: leaving was an intentional career choice, not an escape. DUG clarified what kind of work I want to compound long-term.

First, the output speaks for itself. In 18 months, starting from zero process as essentially a one-person operation, I delivered 55.47% year-over-year revenue growth in the first half of 2025, got featured on the Vision Pro App Store, secured Meta Quest+ entry, and built the Google Android XR partnership. I'm not someone who leaves before the work is done — I left after delivering real results.

Second, it confirmed my direction. I've always been strongest when I learn fast and connect patterns across domains — double-majoring across disciplines, moving from hardware and design into software, then into startups. At DUG, I ramped quickly in XR and delivered outcomes across platforms. The pattern is consistent: I'm fast at entering new spaces, synthesizing what matters, and turning it into strategy and execution. VC is the role where that strength compounds across many companies, rather than being locked into one.

Third, I want to accelerate by learning alongside people with decades of investment judgment. Flint and DUG taught me a lot through doing, but I want to grow in an environment where I'm working closely with great investors and learning how they evaluate founders and markets in real time. Altos is compelling because it's a small, high-bar team where that kind of learning happens naturally.

Fourth, there was a fit reality. I originally joined to help build and scale the business side, but I'm not a game person at heart. Over time I realized I'm more energized by supporting founders and companies across categories than being tied to one product vertical long-term.

So the short tenure reflects clarity, not instability: DUG helped me see that the next chapter I want is VC — especially at Altos — where I can compound learning and impact across many founders.

question: You've experienced many different fields. Is that a strength or weakness for VC?
answer_summary: Breadth is both strength and weakness. Weakness: lacks 10+ years in single domain. Strength: has repeatable evaluation framework across contexts and depth in technical products, enterprise reality, and platform ecosystems.
text:
It's both — and I think the key is being honest about the trade-off, while showing how I manage it.

On the weakness side: I don't have 10+ years in one single domain, so I won't pretend I'm the world's deepest expert in DBMS, AI, or XR. That kind of depth can matter, especially for highly specialized deals. And there's a narrative risk with breadth: if you move too often, people can assume you're unfocused. I'm aware of that, and I'll need to earn trust through consistency and high-quality work at Altos.

On the strength side: In VC, you often have to form conviction in unfamiliar areas quickly. My breadth isn't "I tried a lot of things" — it's that I've repeatedly built a repeatable evaluation framework across very different contexts:

1. Understand the technical architecture — what's actually hard, what's commodity, and what breaks at scale.
2. Map the competitive landscape — who can replicate, who can bundle, and what the true alternative is, including "build in-house."
3. Identify the real user pain and adoption friction — what behavior must change, and why will users stick with it.
4. Pressure-test the business model and GTM — sales cycle, unit economics, dependencies, and what must be true for the company to win.

That framework comes from lived experience: enterprise dynamics at Samsung-level accounts, building products as a founder, and operating in platform-driven ecosystems like Apple, Meta, and Google. It also lets me be a credible conversation partner to founders across multiple categories.

And to be clear, I'm not only broad — I do have depth where it matters for Altos. I'm strongest at the intersection of technical products, enterprise reality, and platform ecosystems — and that's a durable lens for evaluating a lot of modern software and deep-tech startups.

So I'd summarize it like this: breadth is a weakness if it's just curiosity. Breadth is a strength in VC if it's paired with a consistent framework and a few real depth anchors. My goal at Altos is to prove the latter — starting with the areas where my depth is already real: technical products, enterprise dynamics, and platform ecosystems.

question: Please tell me about yourself. Who are you, in your own words?
answer_summary: DJ summarizes his career as bridging deep tech and real-world business. He combines technical depth earned at KAIST with business acumen, having progressed through Zero-to-One founding at Flint and Scaling at DUG. Known for adaptability and reliability with owner's mindset.
text:
Hello, I'm Dong Jae Lee. Career-wise, if I were to summarize my career in one sentence, it would be 'bridging the gap between deep tech and real-world business.' I built my foundation at KAIST, majoring in Mechanical Engineering and Industrial Design. This gave me the literacy to understand complex technology, but my real passion has always been finding the market value within that technology and turning it into a viable, growing business.

My career has been defined by two distinct phases:
First is the 'Zero to One' phase. I co-founded a tech startup called Flint Technologies. As the COO, I experienced the raw reality of building something from nothing. I didn't just strategize; I executed—from defining the MVP and finding Product-Market Fit to securing seed funding and handling investor relations. This experience taught me grit, agility, and how to make critical decisions with limited resources.

Second is the 'Scaling' phase. As the Director at Devs United Games, I focused on global expansion and monetization in the XR space. I led high-stakes partnerships with global platforms like Meta, Apple, and Google.

I also worked on Strategy & Market Research at Changjo Architecture, where I evaluated companies and opportunities across Space, GenAI, and Smart Agriculture sectors.

In short, I offer the best of both worlds: the technical depth to earn the respect of engineering teams, and the business acumen to drive revenue and strategy. I'm looking forward to bringing that versatility to your team.

On a personal level, I am someone who runs toward new challenges, not away from them. My resume reflects a diverse path—from engineering to founding a startup, and then to scaling a gaming business. This isn't because I lack focus, but because I am not afraid of being a beginner again if it means solving a harder, more meaningful problem. I thrive on that steep learning curve.

But no matter where I go, one thing remains constant: my reputation. I take great pride in the fact that my former colleagues—leaders, peers, and engineers alike—are my strongest advocates. They know me as someone who works with an owner's mindset: I don't just 'clock in'; I own the problem until it's solved.

I believe this combination of adaptability and reliability is why people always want to work with me again.

question: Why VC? You could have started another company or joined big tech.
answer_summary: DJ chose VC for leverage and compounding learning, where his pattern-matching strength creates multiplier effects across founders and markets. Comparative advantage, not risk aversion, drives the decision.
text:
Bottom line: I chose VC because it's the role where my highest-leverage edge shows up. I'm not at my best when I'm optimizing one system. I'm at my best when I'm pattern-matching across founders, markets, and products, then turning those insights into clear decisions and faster execution for other people. VC is where that multiplier effect is the most real.

I seriously considered all three paths — big tech, founding again, and VC.

Big tech: great if your edge is being world-class at one narrow domain. But I'm naturally breadth-driven — motivated by understanding how different systems connect. Corporate velocity is slower than my operating rhythm. One domain would underuse my strongest skill: synthesis.

Starting another company: Flint taught me founding is not just building, it's carrying — the uncertainty, the emotional load, the long feedback cycles. I have the scars, and they're useful data. At this stage, the expected downside is not optimal for me. I've realized I'm often better at helping teams navigate hard problems than solving them alone inside one company. Not 'never again' — just 'not the most rational deployment of my strengths right now.'

VC is attractive for two reasons: leverage and compounding learning. I can be a multiplier for founders — diagnosing what's real vs. narrative, asking questions that change outcomes, helping founders make higher-quality decisions faster. And founders listen because I've built a company, seen it fail, shipped at scale, and understand both the product reality and the go-to-market reality.

The compounding learning excites me most. At a startup, knowledge is deep but locked in one domain. In VC, you see dozens of parallel experiments — different founders, market cycles, distribution paths, failure modes. That creates a pattern library that becomes durable and transferable. That's not abstract learning — it directly translates into better sourcing, better underwriting, and better support.

This is comparative advantage, not risk aversion.

question: What role do you want to play at Altos over the next 5 years?
answer_summary: Two-phase vision: Years 1-2 earn trust through output and execution; Years 3-5 lead with conviction. Developed technical DD framework for pre-revenue startups focusing on moat, proprietary compounding, and falsification.
text:
Two-phase vision over the next 5 years at Altos. Years 1-2: my focus is on earning trust through output. I will work to understand Altos' investment thesis deeply, develop strong pattern recognition across the portfolio, and demonstrate consistent high-quality work in sourcing, diligence, and founder support. Years 3-5: once I've built credibility, I want to lead with conviction on areas where I can add unique value.

One specific area I want to develop is a technical diligence framework for pre-revenue startups. For early-stage deep tech or platform companies, traditional due diligence frameworks often fall short. I want to build a framework with three core blocks:

1. The moat claim — what does the founder believe creates defensibility? Is it technical, regulatory, network, or something else? And is that claim actually falsifiable, or is it narrative?

2. Proprietary compounding — if the moat is real, what feedback loops and advantages compound over time? What does the winner look like at 10x scale?

3. Proof and falsification — what evidence would change my mind? What experiments or signals do we need within the next 12-24 months to increase confidence? This is the discipline I learned at Flint: disagree but commit, but back it with data.

This framework comes from my experience building at Flint, learning enterprise dynamics at Tmax, and operating in large platform ecosystems at DUG. I believe this is a differentiating capability for Altos in the pre-revenue space, and it's something I can develop and refine over the next few years.

question: What do you think is the most important thing when starting a company?
answer_summary: Founder philosophy expressed as behavior is the most important thing — the founder's temperament becomes the 'operating system' for everything. Four principles: mission-level commitment + founder chemistry, problem-first over technology, capital efficiency + radical simplification, and winning a focused wedge before building a compounding moat.
text:
If I have to choose one thing, it's founder philosophy expressed as behavior — because in the first 1–2 years there aren't reliable metrics. What you really have is a small group of people making thousands of decisions under uncertainty. The founder's temperament becomes the "operating system" for everything: product quality, speed of iteration, hiring bar, culture, fundraising behavior, and how the company responds when reality disagrees with the plan.

From my own experience, I break it into four principles I've learned the hard way — not from theory.

1) Mission-level commitment and founder chemistry — because the team IS the company.

In early-stage startups, everyone can talk about vision. What differentiates survival is whether the founders treat it like a mission — whether they truly care about the work, the details, and the team when it stops being fun. I saw the opposite risk at Flint: when conviction weakens, everything slows — decision speed, recruiting, product iteration. "Why" isn't a slogan; it's an operating asset.

But individual commitment isn't enough. Product and strategy will change. What must not break is the founders' ability to tell the truth early ("this isn't working"), disagree without ego, and commit decisively. At Flint, when we hit core product friction, the correct response required uncomfortable decisions. If co-founders can't have clean, low-ego conversations at that moment, the company bleeds time and conviction. You can fix product, you can fix GTM, you can fix hiring. It's extremely hard to fix a founding relationship that can't handle truth under pressure.

And this extends beyond founders — organizations are made of people, and execution quality is carried by long-term context. When the people who truly understand the product leave — especially without proper handover — maintenance and iteration become fragile. Founders who build iconic companies don't rely on importing "world-class saviors." They develop internal leaders and retain product ownership.

2) Start with the problem and the customer's reality — not the technology.

This is the most common mistake technical founders make — and I made it even though I knew better.

At Flint, we started with a sophisticated technology (GNN / knowledge graph) and tried to find the best application for it. The vision was intellectually beautiful, but we underestimated how hard it is to get users to repeatedly do the core action. We asked for too much behavior change. The real test isn't "does this look impressive?" — it's "will a normal user do this every day without feeling like homework?"

I learned this earlier in enterprise settings too: in industry, "one successful experiment" doesn't matter unless it fits deployment reality — timeline, risk tolerance, procurement, internal alignment, and accountability when something breaks. A product exists to solve a customer problem in a way the customer can actually adopt.

That changed my founder philosophy permanently: validate the smallest repeatable user action early, and be ruthless about friction.

3) Capital efficiency and radical simplification — constraints force clarity.

One of the most dangerous founder failure modes is confusing fundraising with progress. Founders who are capital-efficient aren't just "spending less" — they're learning faster per dollar. Constraints force you to see what users truly value, what doesn't scale, what costs too much, and what the unit economics are trying to tell you.

Great founders don't waste energy on things they can't control — macro, competitors' announcements, hype cycles. Under stress, weak founders expand scope; strong founders simplify: what can we ship, what can we measure, what can we improve this week, what decision unlocks progress. This sounds basic, but in practice it's a temperament test.

I respect founders who build fundamentals early and don't scale theatrically just to match a promised growth narrative. Profitability — or a credible path to it — keeps the founder in control.

4) Win a focused wedge first, then build a compounding moat.

Most early-stage failures I've seen come from trying to be too broad too early. The founders who win start with a narrow, painful problem where they can be the obvious best solution, then expand outward from that position of strength.

And a real business needs both: customers who pay today, and a reason it keeps winning over time. Moats often form from workflow position and switching costs, data and feedback loops, distribution advantages — especially platform dynamics — or unique operational know-how that compounds. If a company's differentiation is only a feature, it will be copied. A moat is when the advantage compounds with usage, distribution, or time.

My conclusion — and why this matters for how I'd evaluate founders at Altos:

My founder philosophy is: mission-level commitment + low-ego truth-telling + problem-first value creation + capital-efficient fundamentals + focused wedge into compounding moat.

I hold that view because I've lived both sides — I made the classic tech-first mistake at Flint, I've seen customer reality dominate technical elegance in enterprise settings, I've watched platform dynamics and distribution matter operationally at DUG, and I've seen how people and continuity determine whether execution compounds or collapses.

This is also exactly how I'd evaluate founders as a 심사역. Altos invests on the belief that 창업자의 철학이 지표보다 중요 — and I agree, because I've seen firsthand that metrics are lagging indicators of the decisions a founding team already made. The philosophy comes first; the numbers follow.

question: What differentiates a good investor from a bad investor?
answer_summary: A good investor improves a founder's long-term decision quality and execution velocity. A bad investor increases anxiety and noise. Five dimensions: crisis composure (foxhole test), psychological safety, context over KPI panic, signaling discipline for next round, and expanding optionality without ego. Great investors compound founder quality.
text:
At Flint, while raising ~KRW 450M in seed funding and navigating government grants, I experienced both ends of the spectrum.

If I compress it into one principle:

A good investor improves a founder's long-term decision quality and execution velocity.
A bad investor increases anxiety and noise.

That difference becomes most visible in five areas — and the order matters.

1) Crisis Behavior — The Foxhole Test

Anyone can be supportive when growth charts look clean. The real differentiation appears when things break — when runway shortens, experiments fail, or adoption stalls.

Weak investors protect themselves first. They react emotionally, assign blame, or push for premature strategic changes to reduce their own risk.

Strong investors step into the foxhole with you.

At Flint, when our GNN-based knowledge graph hit an adoption ceiling, the team was debating whether the product itself was fundamentally flawed. One investor asked, "When will MAU recover?" That created pressure, but without direction.

Another investor asked, "What does the user data actually say about the friction? If you can't resolve it in eight weeks, what is the highest-leverage use of remaining runway?"

The urgency remained — but the fear disappeared.

Great investors increase urgency without increasing panic. They convert emotion into diagnosis.

2) Psychological Safety — Understanding Founders

Founders carry immense psychological weight. Most are already painfully aware of what isn't working. They spend far more time thinking about how to fix their business than anyone observing from the outside.

Weak investors evaluate output from a distance — almost like third-party consultants.

Strong investors truly try to understand what the founders are going through — the constraints, the tradeoffs, the emotional load — and operate as part of the team, not as external monitors.

I experienced this directly during a difficult pivot. Our metrics were objectively poor, and morale was low. I expected criticism.

Instead, one of our investors said:

"Pivot until you make it. Startups are like this. We invested in the team, not just the metric."

He didn't judge us; he reinforced conviction in the team.

That psychological safety didn't remove pressure. It gave us the stability to keep moving.

Founders don't need comfort. They need investors who understand the weight they are already carrying — and still choose to stand beside them.

3) Context Over KPI Panic

Early-stage metrics are volatile. Everything is noisy.

Inexperienced investors react to dashboards.
Experienced investors use metrics as diagnostic tools.

The best investors I encountered didn't overreact to short-term fluctuations. Instead, they provided pattern recognition — helping us distinguish between normal startup turbulence and structural issues.

They didn't override decisions. They calibrated our thinking.

That institutional memory stabilizes founder judgment during uncertainty.

4) Signaling Discipline — Building the Next Round Before It Exists

A strong early investor thinks at least one round ahead.

Weak investors chase vanity growth or accept messy structures that create signaling risk later.

Strong investors reverse-engineer the next raise. They understand what credible Series A investors evaluate — retention quality, capital efficiency, positioning — and help founders prioritize accordingly. They protect governance. They think about cap table hygiene.

They don't just fund the company.

They make it investable.

5) Expanding Optionality Without Ego

The best investors don't dictate strategy.

Instead of saying, "You should pivot," they say, "Here's what another company tried in a similar situation. It may or may not apply — but I can connect you."

They expand the founder's solution space through network, perspective, and experience — without removing founder agency.

That is partnership.

Final Thought:

Capital is increasingly commoditized.

What isn't commoditized is crisis composure, judgment calibration, psychological alignment, and real partnership.

Bad investors monitor performance.
Good investors provide capital.
Great investors compound founder quality.

Having been on the receiving end — feeling the difference between KPI pressure and diagnostic pressure, between judgment and conviction — I know what that difference feels like.

I want to be the kind of investor I needed when I was building Flint.

question: If you could restart Flint, what would you do differently?
answer_summary: Two changes: (1) Start with urgent pain, not technology — optimize for behavioral inevitability over intellectual elegance. (2) Stay in the game longer with better diagnostics — distinguish 'no demand' from 'too hard to use' and design for Zero-Input Value. The biggest regret is stopping one or two iteration cycles too early.
text:
If I restarted Flint, I would change two things. The product mistakes flowed from the strategic ones.

1. Start With Urgent Pain — Not With Technology

The root mistake was starting from architecture instead of urgency. We built a sophisticated GNN-based knowledge graph because we believed connected knowledge was the future. That belief wasn't wrong — but we anchored the company around technical possibility, not a desperate user problem. We didn't begin with one clearly defined persona — someone with a recurring, painful workflow — and validate pull.

If I restarted Flint: I would not scale infrastructure until one specific user segment showed desperate pull. I would define success as: 'Would this user be genuinely upset if this disappeared tomorrow?' I would manually solve that workflow first, then automate only what proves repeatable.

Technology creates possibility. Urgency creates companies. We optimized for intellectual elegance. I would now optimize for behavioral inevitability.

2. Stay in the Game Longer — With Better Diagnostics

This is the decision I regret most. When growth plateaued, I interpreted it as market rejection. Looking back, I believe we misdiagnosed the failure. We likely didn't fail the market test — we failed the usability test. The value was real, but buried under too much behavioral change.

Today, companies like Pocket, Nessie, and OpenNote are proving that the core belief was valid: knowledge should be persistent, connected, and automatic. The difference wasn't vision — it was iteration depth and friction reduction.

If I restarted Flint: I would distinguish 'no demand' from 'too hard to use.' I would design for Zero-Input Value — the product should deliver an 'aha' moment without the user lifting a finger. I would commit to a predefined iteration runway before concluding the thesis failed.

Staying longer doesn't mean stubbornness. It means improving diagnostic clarity before quitting. I stopped one or two cycles too early. That's on me.

Closing: The biggest shift isn't tactical — it's philosophical. Problem Urgency over Technical Ambition. Behavioral Simplicity over Architectural Purity. Diagnostic Clarity over Early Interpretation. Those lessons were expensive — but they permanently changed how I evaluate startups and how I support founders today.

question: What was the hardest part of fundraising?
answer_summary: The hardest part was bridging the gap between what is true and what is legible. Compressing a '100-hour truth' into a '10-minute narrative' without losing the essence. Two experiences: Flint (novel tech isn't automatically investable) and DUG (fighting lagging market narratives). Key diagnostic: distinguishing false negatives from false positives.
text:
The hardest part of fundraising was bridging the gap between what is true and what is legible.

Founders live in the nuance of their product 24/7. Investors have 30 minutes to pattern-match. My struggle was compressing a '100-hour truth' into a '10-minute narrative' without losing the essence.

I experienced this in two different ways at Flint and DUG.

1) Flint: Novel tech isn't automatically investable. At Flint, we were pitching a pre-revenue product built on GNN-based knowledge graphs. The hardest part was that I was selling complexity, while investors were buying clarity. Early on, I spent too much time explaining how it worked instead of why it had to exist. Investors didn't care about the GNN itself — they cared about the wedge: Who is the desperate user? What pain is acute? Why does this win? Why now? I learned the hard way: if you can't make the wedge legible in 60 seconds, you lose the room — even if the tech is real. The right sequence is: wedge first, architecture second.

2) DUG: Fighting market narratives that lag reality. At DUG, the challenge wasn't product quality — it was sentiment. In Korea, XR had already been labeled 'post-hype' after a wave of metaverse failures. But the reality in the US was different: platform cycles were restarting, Apple and Google were entering, and we had real revenue. Fundraising required translating reality into an investable narrative: 'The platform cycle is restarting. We're not selling a story — we have revenue. We need capital to scale, not to survive.' Fundraising is often less about the world as it is, and more about what the market currently believes is real.

Closing — the investor lesson: This changed how I evaluate founders. When someone struggles to pitch, I now ask a diagnostic question: 'Is this a communication problem — or a product problem?' Some founders have a great business but tell a messy story (false negative). Others tell a great story but have a messy business (false positive). My job as an investor is to look past pitch polish and diagnose the truth underneath — and help the 'messy but great' founders make their wedge legible.

question: How did you feel emotionally when you shut down Flint?
answer_summary: Two emotional waves: identity hit (self-shame, invalidating 3 years) and responsibility (felt like spending others' capital and credibility). Shifted from 'verdict on worth' to 'expensive tuition' — codified failure mechanisms. Became a different operator at DUG: diagnostic over emotional. Earned empathy as an investor, not theoretical.
text:
Honestly, it hit me in two waves.

First was an identity hit.
Shutting down felt like invalidating three years of my life. I didn't just feel disappointed — I felt real self-shame. I had asked talented people to believe in a vision, and I felt I failed to deliver on that promise.
I kept asking myself, "Was this really the best I could do?" Because as a founder, you can always imagine one more iteration, one more push that might've saved it.

Second — and heavier — was responsibility.
Even though our investors were supportive and rational, emotionally it felt personal. I felt like I had spent the capital and credibility of people who trusted me.
I spent nights replaying the tape: What did I miss? What did I delay? What should I have decided earlier?

Then I realized if I stayed in that state, I'd be paralyzed.
So I forced a shift from "What does this say about me?" to "What did this teach me?"

I stopped treating it as a verdict on my worth and started treating it as expensive tuition. I wrote down the failure mechanisms — usability vs. market, thesis vs. execution — not to punish myself, but to codify the lessons.

That's why I became a different operator at DUG: less emotional and more diagnostic, less in love with "cool tech," and more obsessed with customer reality.

It hurt, it humbled me, and it made me serious.
And because I've carried that weight firsthand, I don't romanticize founder struggles — I know how heavy it is.

That's what makes my empathy as an investor earned, not theoretical, and why I can stay steady next to founders when things get hard.

question: Do you see yourself founding again?
answer_summary: Doesn't rule it out but it's not the plan. Two learnings: founding cost is real (10-year commitment), and highest leverage has shifted to helping multiple founders. Committed to VC seriously — compounding judgment, pattern recognition, and founder trust at Altos.
text:
I won't lie — I don't rule it out, but it's not my plan.

Having built a company, I learned two things very clearly.

First, the cost is real. Founding is a 10-year, non-negotiable commitment to one problem. It takes a heavy toll — emotionally, financially, and in opportunity cost. I don't romanticize that anymore. I would only do it again if I found a problem I was uniquely obsessed with — so much that I couldn't not build it.

Second, my highest leverage has changed. I've realized my best work isn't only executing inside one company. It's helping multiple founders think through hard problems, spot blind spots early, and make better decisions faster. That's where I consistently get the most energy.

So my intention is to commit to VC seriously — not as a bridge. I want to spend this phase compounding judgment, pattern recognition, and founder trust at Altos. I want to become genuinely useful at the firm level.

And if I can keep increasing my impact at Altos, I'd rather stay and compound here.

question: After startup failure, was your confidence ever shaken?
answer_summary: Yes — confidence was shaken in two ways: comparison trap (peers progressing while feeling like a 3-year detour) and ego hit (market rewards value, not effort). But confidence changed shape: lost arrogance of 'I know what works,' gained confidence of 'I can handle it when it breaks.' In VC, this is an advantage — doesn't confuse conviction with truth.
text:
Yes — it did. And I say that carefully, because it would actually be strange if it hadn't been shaken at all.

1) The Comparison Trap

The hardest part wasn't the work — it was looking around. While friends were getting promoted at big companies or progressing on very clear career tracks, I felt like I had taken a three-year detour to nowhere. I caught myself thinking: "Did I just waste my prime years?"

It wasn't that I hadn't worked hard. It was realizing that the market doesn't reward effort by default — it rewards value. That gap hit my ego.

2) How My Confidence Changed

But as the dust settled, I realized I didn't lose confidence — it changed shape.

I lost the arrogance of "I know what works." Before Flint, I believed that if I was smart enough and worked hard enough, I could force a product to succeed. Flint humbled me. I learned you can't outwork a market, and you can't brute-force adoption if you're solving the wrong problem.

And I gained the confidence of "I can handle it when it breaks." Even when the worst thing happened — shutting down — I survived. I could look my team in the eye, admit failure, and move forward. I stopped fearing being wrong.

3) Why This Matters for VC

In investing, that's actually an advantage.

Because my ego has been tested, I don't confuse conviction with truth. I'm more skeptical of my initial excitement. I assume I'll be wrong sometimes, and I build processes to find out quickly and correct course.

So yes, it shook me — but it replaced fragile, naïve confidence with quiet, tested confidence. I know I can be wrong, admit it fast, and move forward. And I think that makes me a safer, healthier partner for founders and capital.

question: Can you provide concrete evidence that you were the 'ace' at your previous workplaces?
answer_summary: Two evidence frames: (1) Deliver beyond expectations — DUG (Apple Vision Pro feature, Meta Quest+, Google Android XR from near zero in 18 months, Fishing Haven Apple App Store Awards finalist), TmaxTibero (fast promotion, Samsung DBMS task force, achievement award), Flint (full-stack founder execution, KRW 450M raised), Changjo Architecture (smart farm prototype from zero domain knowledge). (2) People choose to work with me again — DUG CEO recruited from Flint, cofounders reached out first, Changjo CEO re-engaged.
text:
I wouldn't call myself an "ace" — that's for references to decide. But I can answer in two evidence-based ways:

1. I deliver beyond what the role requires.
2. People choose to work with me again.


1) "I deliver beyond expectations."

DUG (Director) — outcomes from near zero
In ~18 months, we secured an Apple Vision Pro App Store feature, entered Meta Quest+, and closed a Google Android XR partnership. These weren't inherited wins. We had no prior Apple relationship; I started from cold outreach and ran partnerships end-to-end — research → outreach → positioning → negotiation → contract closure → execution — while building the internal process essentially from scratch.
Our game Fishing Haven also became a finalist for the 2025 Apple App Store Awards (Games).

TmaxTibero — high-stakes enterprise delivery + fast promotion
At TmaxTibero, I ramped quickly and was promoted faster than typical because I became a reliable owner for high-stakes work. I was on the Samsung DBMS migration task force, where I developed DBMS management tooling and coordinated across Samsung (client), internal delivery, and the core DB team — three groups with conflicting incentives. The work was recognized internally (including an achievement award). The core capability I demonstrated was translating technical requirements into stakeholder decisions and outcomes under pressure.

Flint (co-founder) — full-stack execution under uncertainty
As a co-founder, I led major parts of execution and fundraising. We raised ~KRW 450M and secured government grants while building a technically ambitious product (GNN-based knowledge graph). Even though the company shut down, it shows I can operate in founder mode — framing, fundraising, shipping, making hard calls in ambiguity — and then reflect clearly on what failed and why.

Changjo Architecture — new business groundwork (smart farms)
After Flint, I was brought in by the CEO of Changjo Architecture to explore a new business initiative in smart farms — a domain where neither the company nor I had prior experience. I built early prototypes and hands-on validation (rack systems, cultivation method testing). That became the foundation for an internal smart farm effort that continued as a dedicated initiative/division.


2) "People want to work with me again."

A signal I trust is being pulled back in by people who have seen me operate.

* DUG recruiting: I met Mark Choi (CEO of DUG) while I was at Flint, and he later recruited me into DUG as I was winding Flint down.
* Flint cofounders: My cofounders (Daeheon Jeong and Sanggyun An) reached out to start Flint because they had seen my work ethic and execution firsthand during our undergrad projects.
* Repeat engagement at Changjo: The CEO of Changjo Architecture re-engaged me for additional new-business work after the initial smart farm prototype effort.

I don't claim "ace" as a label. But repeated pull signals are external evidence that people trust me with ambiguous, high-ownership work — and want to collaborate again.

So the evidence is: outcomes delivered from near zero, repeated ownership in high-stakes settings, and repeat "pull" signals. That's the closest objective proof I can offer that I consistently delivered at an "ace" level.

question: Can you give one specific example where you delivered beyond expectations?
answer_summary: Apple Vision Pro partnership at DUG: zero Apple presence to App Store Awards finalist in under 9 months. Cold outreach on LinkedIn, built relationship with Apple Developer Relations Korea, shipped Fishing Haven for Vision Pro alongside Korea launch, earned Apple marketing support. Expanded into ongoing strategic relationship (future titles, Apple Immersive Video, Blackmagic URSA Cine).
text:
One clear example is the Apple Vision Pro partnership at Devs United Games. In under nine months, I took us from zero presence on Apple's platform to becoming an App Store Award finalist.

When I joined DUG in February 2025, Vision Pro had just launched. We were strong on Meta Quest, but on Apple we had no relationships, no product in flight, and no clear path in — and early traction with Apple mattered strategically.

I took ownership of changing that.

I didn't wait for a warm intro. I cold-outreached Apple stakeholders on LinkedIn with a specific case: we had a proven, high-retention title on Quest, and we wanted to bring it to Vision Pro. That led to a connection to Apple Developer Relations in Korea, and from the first meeting I drove a concrete plan — what we'd ship, the timeline, what Apple needed to see, and how we'd execute.

On the product side, it wasn't a simple port — it was a new platform and stack. But we built Fishing Haven for Vision Pro, launched alongside the Korea Vision Pro rollout in November, earned marketing support from Apple, and in 2025 the title became a finalist for the Apple App Store Awards (Games).

What made this beyond expectations is the starting point: there was no existing pipeline. I initiated the relationship cold, built the internal process, aligned the right stakeholders, and delivered a platform-level outcome.

And we didn't treat it as a one-off — we continued into follow-on discussions for future Vision Pro titles and adjacent opportunities around Apple Immersive Video and the emerging ecosystem, including workflows like the Blackmagic URSA Cine Immersive camera.

That's the before-and-after: cold start → shipped product → Apple marketing support → App Store Awards finalist → ongoing strategic relationship.

question: When you're confident about a disagreement, how do you handle it?
answer_summary: Treats disagreement as a decision-quality tool, not a status fight. Three-step framework: ground in goal + decision rights + reversibility, test own confidence and ask what you're missing, convert to experiment. Two examples: pushed DLC strategy with conviction at DUG (25% of revenue), committed fully despite disagreeing on MR prototype (strong platform response).
text:
I try to treat disagreement as a decision-quality tool, not a status fight.

One of the biggest lessons I took from Flint is that even when I feel certain, I can still be wrong — sometimes it's timing, sometimes it's the problem framing, sometimes it's what users will actually do. So when I'm confident, I hold that confidence with humility: the goal is the right outcome, not me being right.

1) I ground the disagreement in the goal and decision rights

First I clarify three things:

* What's the goal we're optimizing for?
* Who is the decision-maker?
* Is this reversible or irreversible?

That prevents opinion debates and forces alignment on what matters.

2) I test my confidence and ask what I might be missing

I ask myself: Am I confident because I have evidence, or because I'm attached?
If I have data, I lead with it. If I don't, I label it as a hypothesis.

Then I assume the other person is rational from their perspective and ask:
"What are you seeing that I'm not?"

3) I try to turn the disagreement into an experiment

Instead of arguing endlessly, I push an option mindset:

* Can we test this quickly?
* Can we timebox it?
* Can we hedge with a smaller bet first?


Example: When I pushed with conviction (DUG DLC strategy)

At DUG, we disagreed on whether to invest in more DLCs versus putting everything into the next title. Some argued we couldn't afford delays; others wanted near-term revenue stability.

I pushed for DLCs because I believed it strengthened the long-term business:

1. It kept users engaged and reduced churn,
2. It created repeatable revenue drops,
3. The team would build a content engine and get faster over time.

We aligned on a clear plan — bi-monthly DLC releases (World Series Tour) — and DLC revenue stabilized at roughly 25% of total revenue, helping defend revenue as the base game aged.


Example: When I committed even though I disagreed

In another case, our CEO wanted to prototype a new MR-focused title despite a small team. My instinct was to focus. But I followed his intuition because he had direct expectations and signal from Apple and Meta about their upcoming roadmap that I didn't have — and he was the decision-maker closest to that information.

So I committed fully. We built the prototype, and when we showed it to platform stakeholders, the response was strong — they were intrigued and wanted to see progress.

So my approach is: strong conviction, low ego — ground it in goals, test my own certainty, and convert disagreement into learning through fast experiments.

question: How would you find great founders before they're on everyone's radar?
answer_summary: Sourcing philosophy: earn the right to be in earliest conversations. Built relationships through KAIST, Apple Developer Academy, startup programs. Founding experience creates trust — people open up. Engages early when someone considers founding. As 심사역, personal network is seed, firm ecosystem is multiplier. Already connected to founders at LBox, Supertone, Vessl AI, Cuckoo, and stealth companies.
text:
The best founders usually do not announce to the market that they are starting a company. They reach out quietly to one or two people they trust. So my sourcing philosophy is to earn the right to be part of those earliest conversations.

I've built relationships across KAIST, my work experience, and the broader startup ecosystem. For example, while scouting talent through the Apple Developer Academy network, I got to know many strong builders early on. I also developed connections through startup programs, consulting circles, and adjacent tech communities. Since I've been interested in startups since my undergraduate years, many people in my close circle today are founders, startup operators, or VCs.

The reason I've been able to build real relationships with these people is, first, that I try to approach people I respect directly and spend time with them — often through coffee chats or dinners rather than purely formal networking. Second, because I've had founding experience myself, people often open up to me about what they are struggling with. I can relate to the ambiguity, pressure, and tradeoffs of building something from scratch, so those conversations often become more honest and substantive. In some cases, I can also be helpful by sharing perspective, talking through difficulties, or giving practical advice.

That proximity means I often hear early when someone is seriously considering leaving to build something. When that happens, I try to engage early — meet them, understand the problem they are drawn to, understand why now, and form an independent view on founder-market fit before the company is visible to the broader market. I think that is the real work of sourcing: not just having broad access, but combining proximity with trust and judgment.

As a 심사역, this compounds — portfolio founders become part of that trust network, and the firm's reputation means founders who don't know me yet are more willing to take that first meeting. My personal network becomes the seed; the firm's ecosystem becomes the multiplier.

I've seen that pattern multiple times already through people connected to companies like LBox, Supertone, Vessl AI, and Cuckoo, and I also know a few people currently preparing companies in stealth. So to me, great sourcing is not about knowing the most people. It is about being close to the right people, building deep trust over time, and earning a place in the earliest conversations.

question: How do you manage stress and maintain mental resilience?
answer_summary: Three mechanisms: (1) separate identity from outcome — treat setbacks as tuition not verdicts, (2) physical discipline — Ashtanga yoga, running, sleep as prerequisites for judgment quality, (3) don't carry stress alone — talk to trusted people honestly. Learned through Flint shutdown experience.
text:
I'll be direct: shutting down Flint was one of the hardest periods of my life. I felt real shame, replayed decisions obsessively, and compared myself to peers whose careers seemed much more linear and stable. That experience taught me that stress management is not optional. It is a professional capability.

There are three things I rely on now.

First, I separate identity from outcome. During Flint, the shutdown felt like a verdict on my worth. Over time, I learned to treat setbacks as expensive tuition rather than character judgments. When I catch myself spiraling into "What does this say about me?", I deliberately shift to "What is this teaching me?" That mental reframing has probably been the single most important change in how I deal with pressure.

Second, I take physical discipline seriously. For me, sleep and exercise are not nice-to-haves; they are prerequisites for clear thinking. I saw very clearly during Flint's hardest periods that when I was mentally and physically depleted, the quality of my judgment dropped. Since then, I've treated physical health as part of the job. I practice Ashtanga yoga, I run, and sometimes the best thing I can do is step away, sleep, and come back with more perspective. Often that reset helps me see a problem more accurately and less emotionally.

Third, I try not to carry stress alone. When things are difficult, I've learned the value of talking to a small number of people I trust and being honest about what is actually weighing on me. I do not think resilience means absorbing everything in silence. I think it means staying functional, reflective, and open enough to keep making good decisions under pressure.

I'm not claiming I'm immune to stress. I'm saying I know my patterns, I have mechanisms that I trust, and I've gone through a genuinely painful failure without becoming defensive or cynical. That experience made me more grounded, more self-aware, and better able to stay steady in uncertain situations.

question: What's the most meaningful thing you did on your own initiative, without anyone asking?
answer_summary: Built a searchable knowledge system around own career — 150+ Q&A entries. Forced intellectual honesty and pattern recognition: discovered career thread (bridging technology and market) that wasn't visible before. Connects to venture instinct: structuring fragmented qualitative information into coherent judgment.
text:
One recent example is building a searchable knowledge system around my own work and reflections.

No one asked me to do it. I started it because I felt a normal resume was too flat — it could list roles and achievements, but it could not really capture how I think, what I've learned, the mistakes I've made, or the patterns across the different things I've done. So I built the system myself from the ground up: I designed the architecture, iterated on the interface many times, and created the knowledge base by writing more than 150 Q&A entries based on my actual work, decisions, and reflections.

It was meaningful to me for two reasons. First, it forced intellectual honesty and pattern recognition. I had to revisit my past work in detail — not just outcomes, but also the reasoning, blind spots, mistakes, and tradeoffs behind them. Through that process, I realized that my career looked scattered from the outside, but underneath it there was actually one consistent thread: I kept moving toward roles where I could bridge technology and market. I had never articulated that so clearly before.

Second, it turned years of experience into something structured, searchable, and reusable. Instead of leaving everything scattered across memory and old documents, I built a system I can keep learning from over time.

I also think that instinct matters in venture. A lot of investing is about taking fragmented qualitative information and forming a coherent view from it. This project came from the same impulse: when something important is unstructured, I want to build the structure myself and use it to improve judgment.

What made it especially meaningful is that no one told me to do it. I saw the gap, defined the project, and kept iterating until it became genuinely useful.
